blocks.text: Every developer has a handful of requests they type over and over, summarize this the same way I always ask for it, review this code with the same checklist I always use, draft a bug report with the same five fields I always fill in.
A prompt template is MCP's answer to that repetition. It is a reusable, named instruction a server hands to a client, with a few blanks left open for whoever is using it to fill in.
This lesson takes the template apart piece by piece: what it is made of, how those blanks get declared, and how a template turns into an actual message the model receives.
1. What a Prompt Template Actually Is

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A prompt template made of a name, a description, and argument placeholders

blocks.text: A prompt template is a piece of reusable text, or a short sequence of messages, that a server defines once and exposes to clients under a stable name.

It is not free floating text a model happens to generate, it is a fixed shape authored ahead of time by whoever built the server, designed to be filled in with a few specific details each time it gets used.
Think of it the way you think of a form letter: the paragraph structure never changes, only the name, the date, and a couple of other fields do.

The whole point of packaging a prompt this way is repeatability. Instead of every user of a server having to remember the exact wording that produces a good bug report or a good code review, the server author writes that wording once, gets it right, and lets everyone reuse it verbatim.

This also means a prompt template can be improved centrally. If the server author finds a better way to phrase the checklist inside a code review prompt, every single user of that server benefits from the improvement the next time they invoke it, without needing to change anything on their own end.
2. The Three Required Fields: Name, Description, Arguments

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Name, description, and arguments are the three required fields

blocks.text: Every prompt template a server declares carries three pieces of information: a name that a client can reference programmatically, a description that explains what the prompt does in plain language, and a list of arguments describing what blanks need to be filled in before the template can be used. These three fields are the entire public contract of a prompt.
2.1 Nothing Else Is Required

Notice how small this contract is. There is no version number, no author field, no category tag mandated by the protocol itself. A server is free to add its own extra metadata, but a client cannot rely on anything beyond name, description, and arguments being present, so any tooling built on top of prompts should treat those three fields as the floor, not assume more will always be there.
3. The Name: A Stable Identifier

A prompt's name is what a client uses to ask for it by a prompts/get call, so it needs to behave like an identifier rather than a piece of prose. Good names are short, lowercase, and use underscores or hyphens consistently, summarize_meeting_notes rather than "Summarize the Meeting Notes for Me". A client will often display the description to a human, but it sends the name to the server, so the name needs to stay stable even if the wording of the description later changes.

Because the name is stable, it is also what a host application uses to remember a prompt across sessions, to bind it to a keyboard shortcut, or to list it in a menu of slash commands. Renaming a prompt is a breaking change for anyone who has built a shortcut around the old name, so treat the name with the same care you would give a public function signature.

A helpful convention borrowed from programming is to namespace names when a server exposes many prompts that cluster into families, git_write_commit_message and git_summarize_branch read clearly as belonging together, compared to two unrelated names that happen to both start with a verb.
4. The Description: Telling a Human What This Prompt Does

The description exists for a human being, not for the model and not for the client's routing logic. It is the sentence a person reads in a prompt picker before deciding whether this is the shortcut they want. A good description says what the prompt produces and, if it is not obvious, what it needs as input. "Produces a concise summary of raw meeting notes, grouped by decision, action item, and open question" tells a user exactly what they are about to get.

blocks.title: Write it for a stranger
blocks.content: A useful test: would a new team member, seeing only the name and description, correctly guess what this prompt does and what to type into its arguments? If not, the description needs more specificity.

blocks.text: Descriptions are also what a client typically uses for simple search or filtering when a server exposes a long list of prompts. A description that front-loads the most distinguishing words, "summarize", "translate", "draft", makes that search meaningfully more useful than one that buries the key verb in the middle of a sentence.
5. Arguments: Placeholders Waiting to Be Filled

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: An argument placeholder waits until it gets filled with a value

blocks.text: Arguments are the blanks in the form letter. Each one has its own name, its own short description, and a flag saying whether it is required. When a client wants to use a prompt, it looks at this argument list, gathers the values it needs, either by asking the user directly or by pulling them from somewhere else in the conversation, and passes them along with the prompts/get call.

Unlike a tool's input schema, a prompt's arguments are always simple, they are described as plain strings with a name and description, not deeply nested JSON structures. This is intentional: prompt arguments are meant to be things a human can type into a small number of text fields, not structured data a program assembles.
5.1 Why Arguments Stay Flat

Keeping arguments flat, one name, one description, one required flag per argument, is a deliberate simplicity constraint. A prompt is meant to be usable from a plain text form in a chat client, and a form full of nested JSON fields would defeat that purpose entirely. If a piece of input genuinely needs rich structure, that is usually a sign the job belongs to a tool instead of a prompt.
6. Declaring Arguments in the Prompt Definition

A server declares its full list of prompts, arguments included, in response to a prompts/list call. This is how a client discovers, ahead of any actual use, exactly what blanks a given template expects. There is no separate schema fetch the way there sometimes is for tools, the argument list returned by prompts/list is the complete and final word on what that prompt needs.

It is worth noting that prompts/list can return prompts without any arguments at all, a fixed template with no blanks whatsoever, such as a daily standup format reminder that never changes. In that case the arguments field is simply an empty list, and prompts/get is called with no arguments map, or an empty one.
7. From Template to Filled Text: The Substitution Step

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A template goes through substitution to become filled text

blocks.text: Once a client has collected concrete values for each argument, it sends them to the server in a prompts/get request. The server then does the actual filling in, substituting each argument's value into wherever that placeholder appears in its internal template text. This step happens entirely on the server, the client never needs to know or care how the substitution is implemented internally.

code.content:
# Server-side template, conceptually
"Please review the following diff, paying special attention to {{focus_area}}:\n\n{{diff}}"

# After substitution with diff="..." and focus_area="security"
"Please review the following diff, paying special attention to security:\n\n<the actual diff text>"

blocks.text: The substitution logic itself is entirely an implementation detail of the server, it might be simple string replacement, a templating engine, or something more elaborate that also pulls in live data. From the client's point of view, none of that matters, only the input arguments and the output messages are part of the contract.
8. The prompts/get Request

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A prompts get request with a name and arguments returns filled messages

blocks.text: A client asks for a filled template with a prompts/get request, passing the prompt's name and a map of argument values. This is the one and only moment a template becomes concrete, before this call it is just a description sitting in a list, after this call it is ready to send to a model.

A well behaved server should validate the arguments it receives in a prompts/get call against what it declared in prompts/list, rejecting a request that is missing a required argument rather than silently filling the template with a blank. This validation step is covered in far more depth later in this module, when we look closely at prompt parameters.
9. What Comes Back: A List of Messages

The response to prompts/get is not a raw string, it is a list of messages, each with a role and content, ready to be dropped straight into a conversation with a model. This matters because a template can produce more than a single user turn, it might return a system style instruction followed by a user turn, or even a short scripted exchange.

Because the shape returned by prompts/get is identical to the shape used everywhere else messages are exchanged in MCP, a client can hand that list straight to whatever code already knows how to send messages to a model, no special case branching required just because the content originated from a prompt rather than being typed directly by a user.
10. Single Argument vs Multiple Argument Templates

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A single argument template is compared against a multiple argument template

blocks.text: The simplest templates take exactly one argument, a block of text to act on, and produce one message. Richer templates take several arguments that each shape the output in a different way, an audience, a tone, a focus area, a target language. There is no hard limit on how many arguments a prompt can declare, but every additional argument is one more thing a user has to think about before they can use the shortcut, so restraint pays off.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Template style","Typical argument count","Example"],"rows":[["Single purpose","1","summarize_text(text)"],["Configurable","2 to 4","code_review(diff, focus_area)"],["Highly parameterized","5 or more","generate_report(data, format, audience, tone, length)"]]}

blocks.text: A useful rule of thumb when designing a new template: if you cannot describe what a given argument does in under ten words, it is probably trying to do too much, and might be better split into two separate, more focused arguments, or even two separate prompts entirely.
11. Optional Arguments and Defaults

Marking an argument required as false tells a client it is fine to omit that value entirely. What happens then is up to the server: it might fall back to a sensible default, it might omit an entire optional clause from the filled template, or it might adjust its wording slightly. A good practice is to describe, right there in the argument description, what happens when the value is left out.

code.content: { "name": "audience", "description": "Who this is for, defaults to a general audience if omitted", "required": false }

blocks.text: A well designed optional argument should never leave the filled template looking obviously broken if it is omitted, no dangling "for audience: " with nothing after the colon. If an optional value is missing, the server should either supply real default wording or quietly drop the clause that depended on it.
12. Templates That Produce More Than One Message

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: One template can expand into several messages at once

blocks.text: Some templates are not one line of filled text but a small scripted conversation, useful for setting up a multi-turn task in one shot. A debugging assistant prompt, for instance, might return a system-style framing message followed by a user message containing the actual stack trace, giving the model both context and the concrete problem in a single prompts/get call.

Multi-message templates are especially useful for onboarding a model into a persona or a mode of operation before handing it the real task, saving a user from having to type that framing instruction by hand every single time.
13. Where Templates Live: Defined on the Server

A prompt template is always authored and stored on the server, never invented by the client. This is what makes prompts shareable and consistent, anyone connecting to that server, regardless of which client application they use, sees the exact same set of templates with the exact same wording. A client's only job is to discover them, present them to a user, collect argument values, and forward the filled result to a model.

This server ownership is also what makes prompts safe to standardize across a team or an organization. A company can ship one internal MCP server with a fixed set of well reviewed prompts, and every engineer, regardless of which client tool they personally prefer, gets access to the exact same vetted wording.
14. A Template Is Not the Same as a String Format

It is tempting to think of a prompt template as nothing more than a Python format string with some blanks. The difference is that a prompt template is a piece of network protocol, discoverable, versioned by name, described for humans, and validated for its arguments, none of which a bare string format gives you. A format string lives inside one program's source code, a prompt template lives on a server and can be reused by any client that speaks MCP.

blocks.text: 15. Designing a Good Template Name and Description

items: Use a verb-first name that reads like an action, summarize_notes rather than notes_summary.
Keep the description to one or two sentences that describe the output, not the implementation.
Name arguments after what they represent, not after their type, diff rather than input_string.
If a prompt has an obvious default behavior when an argument is omitted, say so in that argument's own description.

blocks.text: It also helps to pilot a new template on a real teammate before shipping it broadly. Watch whether they hesitate over what to type into an argument, that hesitation is a signal the argument's description, or the argument itself, needs rethinking.
16. Templates in the Larger MCP Picture

Prompts sit next to tools and resources as one of the three things a server can expose, but they are the only one of the three designed to be triggered directly by a person rather than by the model's own reasoning. A template is the concrete mechanism that makes that possible, a fixed, named, well described shape that turns a user's intent into a properly worded request without asking that user to become a prompt engineer first.

Keep that distinction in mind as the rest of this module builds on it, everything from dynamic content to versioning to security assumes this same basic shape of name, description, and arguments as its starting point.
Worked Example

Imagine a documentation server that wants to offer a "write a changelog entry" shortcut. It declares a template named write_changelog_entry, with a description explaining that it turns a raw commit message into a user-facing changelog line, and two arguments: commit_message, required, and audience, optional, defaulting to "general users".

A user picks this prompt from a menu, pastes in a commit message, leaves audience blank, and the client sends a prompts/get call. The server fills its internal template, falls back to its default audience wording, and returns a single ready-to-send user message.
Notice that nothing about this example required the client to understand changelog formatting rules. All of that knowledge stayed on the server, inside the template, exactly where it belongs.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing a description that explains how the prompt works internally instead of what it produces for the user.
Giving a prompt a vague, noun-only name like report instead of an action-oriented one like generate_weekly_report.
Declaring an argument as required when the template actually works fine without it.
Forgetting to document what happens to an optional argument when it is left out.
Treating the argument list as a place for complex nested structures instead of simple, human-typeable strings.
Changing a template's wording so much that its name no longer describes what it does.

blocks.text: A quick check before publishing a new prompt: read only the name and description aloud to a colleague who has never seen the server, and ask them to guess what arguments it needs. If they guess wrong, tighten the wording.
Practice

Design a prompt template for a customer support server that drafts a polite response to an angry customer email. Decide on the name, write a one-sentence description, and declare its arguments, including at least one required and one optional argument.
Key Takeaway

A prompt template packages a reusable request into three simple parts: a stable name a client can call, a description a human can read, and a small set of argument placeholders that get filled with concrete values through a prompts/get call, producing a ready-to-send list of messages. The template itself always lives on the server, never invented on the fly by the client.

The next lesson looks at what happens when a template is not entirely fixed, prompts whose content or available arguments can shift based on runtime state, and how that differs from the static templates covered here.
